summary.title: A Combined Evidence Approach to Prioritize Nipah Virus Inhibitors
summary.authors: Nishi Kumari, Ayush Upadhyay, Kishan Kalia, Rakesh Kumar, Kanika Tuteja, Rani Paul, Eugenia Covernton, Tina Sharma, Vinod Scaria, Anshu Bhardwaj
summary.executive_summary: Nipah Virus (NiV) is a lethal pathogen with a case fatality rate exceeding 75%, yet no approved treatments exist. Current containment relies on isolation, and existing antivirals like ribavirin show contradictory or limited efficacy. This study addresses the lack of systematic evaluation for Nipah Virus Inhibitors (NVIs) by developing the Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK). The authors conducted a rigorous literature search, curating 182 NVIs, of which 98 are unique small molecule inhibitors. To prioritize these compounds for drug discovery, a combined evidence strategy was employed. This involved computing over 1800 physicochemical descriptors and comparing them against FDA-approved drugs and antiviral libraries. Additionally, compounds were filtered using PAINS and DruLito to assess toxicity and drug-likeness. An independent prioritization was performed based on the robustness of the assays used to identify the inhibitors. The results show that the NVIK library is chemically diverse, with most compounds being cyclic. While many NVIs exhibit physicochemical properties similar to FDA-approved drugs, only a few passed all DruLito filters. Specifically, NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 were highlighted for passing multiple filters and showing drug-like features. The study provides a web-based platform for the community to browse, search, and submit new NVIs, aiming to accelerate the development of therapeutic interventions for NiV and potentially other viruses.

claims.description: A combined evidence approach effectively prioritizes Nipah Virus Inhibitors.
The NVIK platform provides a comprehensive and accessible resource for NVIs.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Nipah Virus (NiV) is a lethal pathogen with a case fatality rate exceeding 75%, yet no approved treatments exist. Current containment relies on isolation, and existing antivirals like ribavirin show contradictory or limited efficacy. This study addresses the lack of systematic evaluation for Nipah Virus Inhibitors (NVIs) by developing the Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK). The authors conducted a rigorous literature search, curating 182 NVIs, of which 98 are unique small molecule inhibitors. To prioritize these compounds for drug discovery, a combined evidence strategy was employed. This involved computing over 1800 physicochemical descriptors and comparing them against FDA-approved drugs and antiviral libraries. Additionally, compounds were filtered using PAINS and DruLito to assess toxicity and drug-likeness. An independent prioritization was performed based on the robustness of the assays used to identify the inhibitors. The results show that the NVIK library is chemically diverse, with most compounds being cyclic. While many NVIs exhibit physicochemical properties similar to FDA-approved drugs, only a few passed all DruLito filters. Specifically, NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 were highlighted for passing multiple filters and showing drug-like features. The study provides a web-based platform for the community to browse, search, and submit new NVIs, aiming to accelerate the development of therapeutic interventions for NiV and potentially other viruses.

Research Context
Nipah Virus is a severe public health concern with high mortality. Current treatment options are limited and ineffective. Ribavirin has shown contradictory results in reducing mortality. Previous inhibitor databases lack systematic evaluation for NiV. There is an urgent need for accelerated R&D for NiV.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to systematically evaluate reported Nipah virus inhibitors. A combined evidence strategy is used to prioritize drug-like compounds. The hypothesis is that robust assays and drug-likeness filters can identify viable candidates. The goal is to create a structured knowledgebase for further development. The platform allows for continuous community curation and analysis.

Methodological Details
PubMed and Google were used to collect inhibitor data. 838 papers were initially shortlisted using the keyword 'Nipah'. A scoring system was applied to prioritize papers for curation. The final knowledgebase contains 182 entries. 98 unique small molecule inhibitors were identified from the 125 small molecule entries. EC50/IC50 values were available for 70 of the compounds. Data quality was ensured by an independent re-curation team. The platform was built using LAMP server technology. 1875 descriptors were calculated using PaDel software. Clustering was performed using Jarvis-Patrick clustering with a 0.15 threshold.

Procedures And Architectures
The NVIK platform allows for simple, query, and structure-based searches. Users can query using SMILES, SDF, and MOL formats. Near neighbours were identified using NNeib version 5.12.0. Clusters were obtained using Jarp version 6.0.2. Visualization was done using customized CIRCOS and Cytoscape. DruLito was used to screen compounds based on eight filters. PAINS filter was applied to study toxicity profiles. Compounds were compared to FDA approved drugs and Enamine antivirals. An independent evaluation based on assay robustness was performed. The web interface provides browsing of physicochemical properties.

Key Results
The IC50/EC50 values range from 0.47 nM to 7562710 nM. Clustering of 98 NVIs resulted in 90 clusters. 84 clusters were singletons, indicating high chemical diversity. 34 NVIs showed structural similarity to 76 FDA approved drugs. Only two of 91 compounds passed all DruLito filters except CMC. 11 NVIs were prioritized based on assay robustness. NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters. NVIC0048 displayed high overlap with physicochemical parameter ranges. NVIC0032 exhibited better activity among the shortlisted compounds. The platform currently hosts 182 NVIs with 98 small molecules.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The high diversity of NVIs offers a wide spectrum for drug development. Near neighbours with different molecular weights may share pharmacophore features. Prioritization based on assay robustness adds a layer of reliability. The platform serves as a centralized resource for the scientific community. These compounds may also be useful for other viruses.

Contradictions And Limitations
Ribavirin results are contradictory, with optimistic ones below 50% reduction. 57 entries were peptides or lacked complete information. Only a few compounds passed all DruLito filters. The study relies on literature curation, which may have gaps. No clinical trials are currently underway for NiV.

Claims
A combined evidence approach effectively prioritizes Nipah Virus Inhibitors. 11 NVIs were prioritized based on assay robustness. 3 compounds passed 6 DruLito filters. Only two compounds passed all filters except CMC. This strategy can accelerate drug discovery for NiV.
The NVIK platform provides a comprehensive and accessible resource for NVIs. The platform allows submission of new inhibitors. It contains 182 entries with detailed physicochemical data. Some entries lack complete information. It facilitates community-driven curation and analysis.

Data And Code Availability
Data is available at http://vinodscaria.rnabiology.org/nipah. The platform allows for public submission of new compounds.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Data quality was checked by an independent team. Errors were marked and verified by both teams.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the unique fields in the database. Figure 2 depicts the distribution of physicochemical properties. Figure 3 compares NVIs with FDA approved drugs and antivirals. Figure 4 shows the DruLito filter results. Table 2 lists the prioritized NVIs and their properties.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the NVIK knowledgebase with 182 NVIs. 2. The strongest evidence is the prioritization of 11 NVIs via robust assays. 3. The future path is community-driven curation and drug development.
